issues.legal_issue: A revenue authority may distrain a defaulter’s movable property even when it is in the custody and possession of an executing court.
material_facts: A house belonging to a debtor was sold in execution of a decree, and the sale proceeds were deposited with the executing court.
The revenue authority sought to distrain part of those proceeds for the debtor’s unpaid sales tax.
The authority acted under a provision empowering distraint and sale of a defaulter’s movable property.
issues.conclusion: The distraint procedure was not invalid merely because the movable property was in the custody and possession of the court; the provision permitted distraint of the sale proceeds.
issues.legal_principle: Section 119 of the Hyderabad Land Revenue Act, read with section 13(2) of the Hyderabad General Sales Tax Act, authorises recovery of tax as arrears of land revenue and permits distraint of the defaulter’s movable property. Section 119 is expressed generally and contains no restriction excluding movable property in a court’s custody.

predicates.appeal_challenging_distraint_order: A party challenged a revenue authority’s distraint order in an appeal.
predicates.proceeds_of_defaulters_property_held_by_: Property belonging to a debtor was sold in execution, and the resulting movable proceeds were held by the executing court.
predicates.authority_to_distrain_defaulters_movable: The governing recovery scheme authorised the revenue authority to distrain the debtor’s movable property.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges distraint and the proceeds of a debtor’s property are held by a court under a scheme authorising distraint of the debtor’s movable property, those proceeds may be distrained.

issues.legal_issue: Treating a tax as recoverable by the procedure for collecting land revenue does not give the tax the statutory priority accorded to land revenue.
material_facts: The debtor owed unpaid sales tax to the government and owed a decree debt to a creditor.
The creditor’s decree was being executed against a house furnished as security, and the sale proceeds were deposited in court.
The sales-tax law permitted recovery of the tax as arrears of land revenue.
The land-revenue statute provided priority for demands for land revenue, while separately permitting recovery procedures to be used for other taxes.
issues.conclusion: The government had no statutory priority for the sales-tax arrears over the creditor’s claim; the land-revenue recovery procedure did not extend the substantive priority for land revenue to other taxes.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(2) of the Hyderabad General Sales Tax Act made sales tax recoverable as arrears of land revenue. Under sections 116 and 144 of the Hyderabad Land Revenue Act, the recovery procedures could apply to taxes, but section 104’s substantive priority applied only to land revenue. The court therefore distinguished the recovery procedure from the rule of priority.

predicates.proceeding_involving_competing_tax_and_d: A proceeding concerned competing claims to property between the government for unpaid tax and a creditor enforcing a decree.
predicates.tax_recoverable_by_land_revenue_procedur: The applicable tax law directed that the tax could be recovered using the procedure for collecting land revenue.
predicates.priority_clause_confined_to_land_revenue: The applicable priority clause gave precedence to demands for land revenue, while other taxes were included only for recovery purposes.

issues.definition: When competing tax and decree claims arise, a tax recoverable by land-revenue procedures does not take statutory priority if the priority clause is confined to land revenue.

issues.legal_issue: The common-law priority of government debts cannot be applied as continuing law without proof that it had been judicially recognised in the relevant territory before constitutional continuity began.
material_facts: The government claimed priority for unpaid sales tax under the common-law doctrine of priority of Crown debts, independently of the land-revenue statute.
The relevant territory had been a princely state before becoming part of the Indian Republic.

Despite time being allowed to produce supporting material, the government did not establish that courts in that territory had judicially recognised the doctrine before the Constitution came into force.
issues.conclusion: The government could not claim priority under the common-law doctrine because its prior judicial recognition in the relevant territory had not been proved, and it therefore was not shown to be a law in force continued by Article 372(1).
issues.legal_principle: Article 372(1) continues laws in force at the commencement of the Constitution. Builders Supply Corporation v. Union of India recognised the doctrine’s continuation where it had been judicially recognised in the relevant territory. Superintendent & Remembrancer of Legal Affairs, West Bengal v. The Corporation of Calcutta concerned a distinct rule of statutory construction and did not displace Builders Supply. In this case, however, judicial recognition of the priority doctrine in the relevant territory before constitutional commencement was not proved.

predicates.proceeding_claiming_common_law_governmen: A proceeding involved a government claim to priority over a private debt based on the common-law doctrine of priority of government debts.
predicates.competing_private_debt_claim: A private creditor also asserted a claim against the debtor’s property.
predicates.preconstitutional_local_judicial_recogni: The government did not establish that courts in the relevant territory had judicially recognised the doctrine before constitutional continuity began.

issues.definition: When the government claims common-law debt priority against a private creditor but prior judicial recognition of that doctrine in the relevant territory is not established, the doctrine is not available as continued law.
